passages.t: Children of the LORD, even in grief
passages.happening:
Moses begins with who Israel is. “You are sons of the LORD your God; do not cut yourselves or shave your foreheads on behalf of the dead, for you are a people holy to the LORD your God” (verses 1-2).

He repeats what he said in chapter 7. “The LORD has chosen you to be a people for His prized possession out of all the peoples on the face of the earth” (verse 2).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is about ordinary things: how a family mourns, what it eats, and what it does with a tenth of its harvest. It starts from a relationship. Israel's people are God's children. What follows is how his children live.

The two acts forbidden in verse 1 were mourning customs of the ancient world. People marked their grief on their bodies. Such rites could be tied to the worship of the dead or to winning the favor of the gods. The prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel acted in the same way in their worship.

Israel was not forbidden to grieve. The Old Testament is full of weeping, and it gives whole psalms to it. What Israel was told is that its grief must not borrow those rites. A child of the living God does not have to buy the attention of heaven with pain.

‘Holy’ means set apart, belonging to God. The word stands at the beginning of this section and again at verse 21. Israel is holy because God chose it for himself. It is not holy because it is morally better than others.
passages.later:
Leviticus gives the same rule: “You must not make any cuts in your bodies for the dead” (Leviticus 19:28).

The book of Kings tells of the prophets of Baal doing the same on Mount Carmel, ‘as was their custom’ (1 Kings 18:28).

Paul does not tell Christians not to grieve. He writes so that ‘you will not grieve like the rest, who are without hope’ (1 Thessalonians 4:13).
passages.hard:
Does this verse mean that a believer should not show grief?

No. The verse forbids two rites of the ancient world. It does not forbid tears, and it does not ask anyone to hide sorrow. The people of the Bible weep openly, and Jesus himself wept at a friend's grave (John 11:35).

If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, or you feel you do not want to go on, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. You do not have to carry it alone. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Moses says, ‘You are sons of the LORD your God’, before he gives a single rule. Ask whether you obey God as his child or as someone trying to win a place. And if you are grieving, ask whether you have let yourself bring that grief to him as it is.

passages.t: Clean and unclean: what Israel may eat
passages.happening:
“You must not eat any detestable thing” (verse 3). Then Moses lists what may be eaten.

Of land animals: the ox, the sheep, the goat, and wild animals such as deer and gazelle. The test is simple. “You may eat any animal that has a split hoof divided in two and that chews the cud” (verse 6). Animals with only one of the two marks are excluded: the camel, the rabbit, the rock badger, and the pig. ‘It is unclean for you’ (verse 8).

Of creatures in the water, ‘you may eat anything with fins and scales’ (verse 9). Of birds, any clean bird may be eaten, and a list of forbidden birds follows, many of them birds that hunt or eat dead flesh (verses 11-18). Flying insects are unclean (verse 19).

An animal found dead is not to be eaten, though it may be given or sold to a foreigner. “For you are a holy people belonging to the LORD your God. You must not cook a young goat in its mother’s milk” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
A fuller list is in Leviticus 11. This shorter one is addressed to ordinary households. Many of the bird names are rare Hebrew words, and translators are not sure of several.

Notice the repeated words ‘for you’. The animals are not called evil. They are God's creatures. In the Old Testament ‘unclean’ is not the same as sinful or dirty. It is a ritual status that affects coming to worship. These animals were simply not to be eaten by Israel.

Verse 21 shows this clearly. The carcass an Israelite may not eat may be given to a foreigner, ‘and he may eat it’. The food laws were not a diet for all people. They marked Israel's calling.

Why these animals and not others? The chapter gives no reason for any one of them, and readers have offered several. Some point to health, though that does not explain every case. Some note that certain animals, such as the pig, were used in the worship of other gods. The anthropologist Mary Douglas argued in 1966 that clean animals are those that fit their realm completely, and unclean ones blur the lines, so that the laws taught wholeness and order. Others see the laws mainly as a boundary, a daily reminder at every meal that Israel was set apart. These views can be held together. The reason the text itself gives is holiness.

There is one piece of evidence from the ground. Pig bones are common at many sites of this period on the coast and are rare or missing at sites in the hills where Israelites settled. Some archaeologists take this as a sign that avoiding pork marked Israel early. Others warn that diet also depended on land and economy.

The last rule, about a young goat and its mother's milk, has puzzled readers for centuries. The medieval Jewish scholar Maimonides thought it opposed a pagan rite. Others see a law of compassion, which refuses to mix the source of a young animal's life with its death. From this rule Jewish tradition developed the practice of keeping meat and dairy foods apart.

None of this treats the food laws as foolish. God gave them, and they did their work. Jewish families who keep them today are honoring the God of Abraham.
passages.later:
Leviticus gives the reason behind the list: “be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44).

Jesus taught that ‘nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him’, and Mark adds, “(Thus all foods are clean.)” (Mark 7:18-19). The note on Mark 7 sets out how that sentence is read.

Peter was shown animals of every kind in a vision and told, “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean” (Acts 10:15). He understood it to be about people: ‘God has shown me that I should not call any man impure or unclean’ (Acts 10:28).

Paul writes, “For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17).
passages.hard:
Do the food laws still apply?

Jewish tradition continues to keep them as part of the covenant with Israel.

Most Christian traditions hold that Jesus and the apostles declared all foods clean for believers, so that these laws no longer bind, though they still teach that God's people are to be set apart. They point to Mark 7:19, to Acts 10 and to Romans 14.

Some Christians do keep these laws. Seventh-day Adventists avoid the meats this chapter calls unclean. Many Jewish believers in Jesus keep the food laws as part of their Jewish life. Paul asked believers on each side not to judge the other: “The one who eats everything must not belittle the one who does not, and the one who does not eat everything must not judge the one who does, for God has accepted him” (Romans 14:3).

The site's page on which Old Testament laws Christians keep goes further.
passages.asks: At every meal Israel was reminded whose it was. Ask what in your ordinary day reminds you that you belong to God. And ask whether there is any part of daily life, your table, your money or your free time, that you think of as having nothing to do with him.

passages.t: The tithe: a feast, and food for those without land
passages.happening:
“You must be sure to set aside a tenth of all the produce brought forth each year from your fields” (verse 22).

The family is to take that tenth to the place God chooses and eat it there, ‘so that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always’ (verse 23). If the place is too far to carry it, they may sell it, take the money, and buy food there, ‘cattle, sheep, wine, strong drink, or anything you wish’. “You are to feast there in the presence of the LORD your God and rejoice with your household” (verse 26). They must not neglect the Levite (verse 27).

Every third year the tenth is handled differently. It stays in the home town and is stored there. “Then the Levite (because he has no portion or inheritance among you), the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow within your gates may come and eat and be satisfied” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
A tithe is a tenth. In the ancient world a tenth was a common payment, owed to kings or to temples.

Deuteronomy does something unexpected with it. In most years the tithe is a meal. The family that grew the crop eats it before God, with joy. The first lesson of giving in this chapter is thanksgiving. Israel is to enjoy what God has given, in his presence, and so ‘learn to fear’ him. Reverence is learned at a feast.

The rule about money is practical. A farmer far from the sanctuary could not carry a tenth of his harvest. He may turn it into silver and buy food when he arrives. The law bends to fit real life, as it did with meat in chapter 12.

Every third year the tithe becomes something like a food store for the town. Four groups are named: the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan and the widow. What they share is that they have no land. In a farming society, no land meant no harvest. The law does not leave their food to the kindness of neighbors on a good day. It writes it into the calendar. And they are to ‘eat and be satisfied’, which is the word used of Israel's own plenty in chapter 8.

Numbers 18 speaks of the tithe as the support of the Levites. Deuteronomy stresses the feast and the poor.
passages.later:
Abraham gave a tenth long before the law (Genesis 14:20), and Jacob vowed one (Genesis 28:22).

Jesus spoke of people who paid tithes of their smallest garden herbs. “But you have disregarded the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness. You should have practiced the latter, without neglecting the former” (Matthew 23:23).

Paul gives the church no figure. He writes, “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
passages.hard:
Must Christians tithe?

Christians differ. Some hold that the tenth is a standing rule for God's people, older than Sinai, since Abraham and Jacob gave it. Others hold that the tithe belonged to the law of Moses, with its Levites and its sanctuary, and that the New Testament sets no figure but calls for giving that is free, generous and glad. Many who take the second view still treat a tenth as a wise place to begin. These notes take no side.

Whatever a reader's view, this chapter gives no one the right to press money out of people in God's name. The tithe here is eaten with joy and shared with the poor.
passages.asks: In this chapter giving begins as a feast of thanks and ends as food for people with no land. Ask whether your giving has joy in it, and whether any of it reaches the people in your town who have least. And ask what regular habit, written into your calendar and not left to mood, would make your generosity dependable.
